scenes.tts: If an adult brain made a new neuron, how would you ever know it was new?
scenes.visual: Title card: Two Facts in One Cell. An adult rat brain in outline, the hippocampus highlighted.
scenes.narration: If an adult brain made a new neuron, how would you ever know it was new?

scenes.tts: The old rule: the neurons you are born with are the ones you keep.
scenes.visual: Caption card: the neurons you are born with are the neurons you keep.
scenes.narration: The old rule: the neurons you are born with are the ones you keep.

scenes.tts: A cell copies its DNA before it divides. A finished neuron normally does not copy its DNA again.
scenes.visual: A dividing cell beside a mature neuron. Only the dividing cell's chromosomes duplicate.
scenes.narration: A cell copies its DNA before it divides. A finished neuron normally does not copy its DNA again.

scenes.tts: So give an animal tagged thymidine, a DNA building block. Cells copying their DNA build it in.
scenes.visual: Labelled thymidine drawn as coloured bases; they enter only the dividing cell's DNA, not the mature neuron's.
scenes.narration: So give an animal tagged thymidine, a DNA building block. Cells copying their DNA build it in.

scenes.tts: A labelled cell can divide again, and each daughter carries about half the label.
scenes.visual: A two-division family tree. The label is halved at each division: full, half, quarter. Drawn as halving, not stamped once.
scenes.narration: A labelled cell can divide again, and each daughter carries about half the label.

scenes.tts: So the label dates the DNA. A strongly labelled neuron was most likely born that day, or later.
scenes.visual: Caption: the label dates the DNA. Most likely born that day, or later.
scenes.narration: So the label dates the DNA. A strongly labelled neuron was most likely born that day, or later.

scenes.tts: DNA repair, or a dying cell copying its DNA, can add label too. Studies need controls.
scenes.visual: A non-dividing neuron picks up a faint speck of label at a repaired stretch of DNA. Caption: label without division; controls needed.
scenes.narration: DNA repair, or a dying cell copying its DNA, can add label too. Studies need controls.

scenes.tts: In the nineteen sixties, Joseph Altman found labelled cells in the dentate gyrus of rats.
scenes.caption: In the 1960s, Joseph Altman found labelled cells in the dentate gyrus of rats.
scenes.visual: A rat dentate gyrus section. Dark silver grains over one nucleus, a glial cell pressed against it. Credit: Altman, 1960s, tritiated thymidine.
scenes.narration: In the 1960s, Joseph Altman found labelled cells in the dentate gyrus of rats.

scenes.tts: Pause and predict. Is the labelled cell a neuron?
scenes.visual: Question card: is the labelled cell a neuron?
scenes.narration: Pause and predict. Is the labelled cell a neuron?

scenes.tts: The light microscope could not tell. The grains might belong to a glial cell pressed against a neuron.
scenes.visual: Zoom on the nucleus and the glial cell beside it; a question mark over which one carries the grains.
scenes.narration: The light microscope could not tell. The grains might belong to a glial cell pressed against a neuron.

scenes.tts: A birth record, but no identity. The claims were largely set aside for years.
scenes.visual: Two-box card: birth record, ticked; neuron identity, empty.
scenes.narration: A birth record, but no identity. The claims were largely set aside for years.

scenes.tts: In nineteen seventy-seven, electron microscopy showed that labelled cells in adult rats were neurons.
scenes.caption: In 1977, electron microscopy showed that labelled cells in adult rats were neurons.
scenes.visual: Schematic of a labelled neuron seen by electron microscopy. Credit: Kaplan and Hinds, 1977, rat.
scenes.narration: In 1977, electron microscopy showed that labelled cells in adult rats were neurons.

scenes.tts: Then came B R D U, a thymidine look-alike that an antibody can detect.
scenes.caption: Then came BrdU, a thymidine look-alike that an antibody can detect.
scenes.visual: The thymidine base beside the BrdU base: a bromine where thymidine has a methyl group.
scenes.narration: Then came BrdU, a thymidine look-alike that an antibody can detect.

scenes.tts: One cell can now be stained twice, for B R D U and for the neuron protein new N.
scenes.caption: One cell can now be stained twice, for BrdU and for the neuron protein NeuN.
scenes.visual: A split cell: BrdU stain in one colour, NeuN stain in a second colour, overlapping in one nucleus.
scenes.narration: One cell can now be stained twice, for BrdU and for the neuron protein NeuN.

scenes.tts: That is the rule for this lesson. A neuron counts as new only when the same cells carry two facts.
scenes.visual: The rule card builds: two facts, same cells.
scenes.narration: That is the rule for this lesson. A neuron counts as new only when the same cells carry two facts.

scenes.tts: A birth record, showing their DNA was copied at a known time, so they were most likely born then or later. And a neuron identity.
scenes.visual: Rule card: birth record (most likely born then or later), plus neuron identity.
scenes.narration: A birth record, showing their DNA was copied at a known time, so they were most likely born then or later. And a neuron identity.

scenes.tts: A young-neuron marker, such as doublecortin, tells you a cell's state, not when it was born.
scenes.visual: A third box beside the rule card: young-neuron marker, doublecortin. Label: a state, not a birth date.
scenes.narration: A young-neuron marker, such as doublecortin, tells you a cell's state, not when it was born.

scenes.tts: Takeaway: two facts in the same cells.
scenes.visual: Closing card: birth record plus neuron identity, in the same cells.
scenes.narration: Takeaway: two facts in the same cells.
